title: L14 · Muscular System II
subtitle: Nervous system, NMJ, contraction, energy, fiber types, twitches

lines.text: The nervous system is the master control system.
**Sensory input**: receptors notice changes.
**Integration**: the system processes and decides.
**Motor output**: it activates muscles and glands.
The **CNS** is the brain and spinal cord. It's the command center.
The **PNS** is the spinal and cranial nerves.
Sensory, or **afferent**, nerves carry signals to the CNS.
Motor, or **efferent**, nerves carry signals out to effectors.
Somatic motor is voluntary. Autonomic motor is involuntary: sympathetic and parasympathetic.
**Dendrites** bring signals to the **cell body**.
The **axon** carries them away to other cells.
**Multipolar** neurons have many dendrites. All motor neurons are multipolar.
Sensory neurons are unipolar. Interneurons live only in the CNS.

scenes.title: Motor units and the all-or-nothing principle

lines.text: A muscle fiber contracts completely or not at all. That's **all-or-nothing**.
It needs a **threshold** stimulus.
A **motor unit** is one neuron and all the fibers it controls.
Small units give fine control, like the eye. Large units give power, like the thigh.
**Recruitment** adds more motor units for more force.
The **synaptic knob** holds vesicles of acetylcholine.
The **synaptic cleft** is the gap. It holds the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine.
The **motor end plate** is folded muscle membrane covered in receptors.
The impulse reaches the knob. Calcium channels open, and **calcium** rushes in.
Vesicles release acetylcholine into the cleft.
It binds the end plate. Sodium flows in. Potassium flows out.
More sodium enters than potassium leaves. That's **depolarization**.
An **action potential** races along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules.
The action potential reaches the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
It releases calcium into the cytosol.
Calcium binds **troponin**.
Troponin pulls **tropomyosin** off the binding sites on actin.
**Attach**: myosin heads grab actin.
**Power stroke**: myosin pulls actin toward the center.
**Release**: ATP binds myosin, and it lets go.
**Reset**: ATP splits and re-cocks the head.
When signals stop, calcium goes back into the SR, and the muscle relaxes.
With no ATP, heads can't let go. That's rigor mortis.
ATP is the only energy muscle uses directly.
**Creatine phosphate** is fastest. No oxygen. About 10 to 15 seconds.
**Anaerobic** glycolysis makes 2 ATP per glucose. No oxygen. 30 to 40 seconds. It leaves lactic acid.
**Aerobic** respiration in the mitochondria makes about 32 ATP. It needs oxygen and lasts for hours.
It supplies 95 percent of the ATP for muscle.
Fatigue is when a muscle can't contract even when stimulated.
Causes include **oxygen deficit** and **ion imbalance** of calcium and potassium.
Also **lactic acid** buildup, low ATP, and running out of acetylcholine.
**Slow oxidative** fibers are dark red and fatigue resistant. Posture and marathons.
**Fast oxidative** fibers are light red. Walking and biking. They're the least common.
**Fast glycolytic** fibers are white and tire quickly. Sprints and lifting. They're the most common.
A twitch is one contraction to one stimulus.
The **latent** period comes first. Calcium is being released.
Then the **contraction** period, then the **relaxation** period.
During the **refractory** period, the muscle won't respond.
A whole muscle can grade its force.
Rapid stimuli add up. That's **summation**.
It becomes **unfused tetanus**, then smooth **fused tetanus**.
Recruiting more fibers adds force too.
**Muscle tone** is the slight tension a resting muscle always keeps.
**Isometric**: the muscle tenses but doesn't change length.
Isotonic contractions move.
**Concentric**: the muscle shortens.
**Eccentric**: the muscle lengthens while it contracts.
**Endurance** exercise adds mitochondria and blood supply.
**Resistance** exercise adds actin and myosin. Fibers get bigger.
**Hypertrophy** is growth with more function. **Atrophy** is shrinking.
Muscle slowly declines from the mid thirties.
